title: NASA, CLPS, and the satellite-systems counterparty addition
body:
## A contract ceiling and a crowded pool

When NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme was structured in the late 2010s, the agency borrowed deliberately from its own playbook. Like the Commercial Resupply Services contracts that underwrote SpaceX's early Falcon 9 cadence, and the Commercial Crew programme that eventually put American astronauts back on an American rocket, CLPS was designed to spread risk across a pool of pre-qualified vendors, award task orders mission by mission, and let competition drive cost down over time. The total programme ceiling was set at $4.82 billion — a number large enough to sustain a commercial ecosystem across the Artemis decade, yet structured so that no single awardee could treat it as a guaranteed revenue stream. Intuitive Machines entered that pool as one of a handful of companies, won the first operational lunar surface delivery, and has since accumulated more task-order value than any competitor in the programme.

The $4.82 billion ceiling is best understood as an addressable opportunity, not a committed backlog. NASA guarantees only a fraction of the pool's value in near-term awards — roughly $150 million of near-term committed value was disclosed in the company's annual filings — and task orders are competed among the awardees. That structure keeps NASA's cost discipline intact while giving the commercial awardees a reason to invest in launch cadence, reliability, and lunar surface engineering. For Intuitive Machines, the most consequential single task order awarded to date was the $180.4 million IM-5 contract, which calls for the delivery of seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the cargo-class Nova-D lander — a platform one size larger than the Nova-C vehicles that carried the first two missions. [SEC 10-K, LUNR FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm)

## The mission catalog: two landings, three more in the pipeline

The operational record begins on 22 February 2024, when the IM-1 lander — call sign *Odysseus*, a Nova-C class vehicle launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 — touched down in the Malapert A crater region near the lunar south pole. The landing was not clean. A sensor switch left in the wrong position during launch preparation disabled the vehicle's primary laser rangefinders; engineers improvised a fix using an experimental NASA instrument on board, and *Odysseus* reached the surface but came to rest on its side, a landing-leg having snagged on the terrain. Despite the orientation, several payloads operated. The company had done what no private enterprise had ever done: it landed a spacecraft on the Moon.

IM-2, the *Athena* mission, followed in the first quarter of 2025 — again a Nova-C class lander, again reaching the lunar surface with operational complications. The pattern of two missions that technically achieved surface contact but encountered engineering difficulties is the acknowledged vulnerability in the investment thesis: the company is still learning, in the most unforgiving environment a vehicle can encounter, and the learning carries real cost. As of the 23 May 2026 snapshot, IM-3 was in active preparation and IM-4 in planning, with the Nova-D-class IM-5 mission — the largest and most complex in the catalogue — carrying the $180.4 million task order and representing the programme's first step toward genuine cargo delivery at scale.

The mission sequence matters for revenue recognition as much as for operational credibility. NASA milestone payments are recognised against task-order completion milestones, producing a revenue profile that looks lumpy to anyone accustomed to a stable SaaS or defence-services contract. The company's fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $44.8 million was down roughly 18 percent year-on-year, reflecting the reality that IM-1 mission revenue had been substantially recognised in FY2024 and FY2025 was a period of mission preparation rather than delivery. Full-year FY2025 revenue fell in the $250 million to $300 million range. The cadence of task-order awards and the pace of mission execution will govern whether the FY2026 outlook of $900 million to $1 billion in revenue proves achievable on the lunar-delivery side of the ledger.

## Secondary customers and national-security adjacency

Beyond CLPS, Intuitive Machines has cultivated relationships with the national-security customer base that shares an interest in cislunar domain awareness. The Department of Defense, DARPA, and the US Space Force have each engaged the company as a counterparty — the rationale converging on the observation that the same telemetry, tracking, and control capability required for lunar surface operations is exactly what the defence establishment needs to understand the cislunar environment that great-power competition is beginning to contest.

The company's proprietary lunar telemetry, tracking, and control infrastructure — built to support its own missions — represents a potential separate revenue line for government customers who need coverage in cislunar space but lack the assets to provide it themselves. This is the kind of dual-use infrastructure whose strategic value is difficult to capture in a quarterly earnings release but which has historically commanded durable government revenue in analogous programmes.

## The competitive pool: Firefly advances, Astrobotic stumbles

The CLPS awardee pool is small, and the competitive dynamics have already been shaped by mission outcomes as much as by contract awards. Astrobotic Technology, a Pittsburgh-based private company and one of the earliest CLPS awardees, conducted an attempted lunar delivery with its Peregrine lander in January 2024. The mission ended before reaching the lunar surface when a propulsion failure prevented the vehicle from completing its trajectory. The Peregrine failure underscored the difficulty of what Intuitive Machines was attempting — and amplified the significance of *Odysseus* completing its approach two weeks later.

Firefly Aerospace, which trades publicly under the ticker FLY, achieved a successful landing with its Blue Ghost lander in 2025, marking the second private lunar surface delivery in the CLPS era and establishing Firefly as a credible long-run competitor for task orders. The programme now has two operational awardees, and NASA's stated preference for maintaining a competitive pool means that Firefly's success makes it more likely — not less — that Intuitive Machines will continue to face genuine competition for future task orders.

The broader competitive map also includes SpaceX and Blue Origin, though their positions are structurally different. SpaceX provides launch services rather than competing in payload delivery — Falcon 9 flew both IM-1 and is the likely vehicle for subsequent Nova-C missions — and its Starship vehicle anchors the NASA Human Landing System as one of the agency's sustained lunar lander platforms. Blue Origin is developing the Blue Moon lander under the HLS programme. Neither company is a direct CLPS competitor today, but both represent potential future entrants into the lunar logistics market if the economics justify vertical integration beyond launch services.

The traditional aerospace primes — Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, and Raytheon — are not CLPS competitors in their own right, but they become increasingly relevant as Intuitive Machines' scope expands. The Lanteris acquisition is where this competitive overlap begins to materialise.

## Lanteris and the counterparty addition

The $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems — structured as $450 million in cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected close in the first quarter of 2026 — is the transaction that transforms Intuitive Machines' counterparty map. [SEC EDGAR, LUNR FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm)

Lanteris brought with it a satellite-systems customer book with institutional relationships cultivated over years of work with Boeing Satellite Systems International. Chris Johnson, who led Lanteris as chief executive and had previously served as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International, moved into the combined company as President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines. The significance of that pedigree is not ceremonial: Boeing Satellite Systems International is one of the largest commercial satellite bus manufacturers in the world, and the customer relationships Johnson carried represent a direct bridge into the commercial and government satellite-systems procurement network.

Post-Lanteris, Intuitive Machines' total backlog reached $943 million — a figure that reflects the combined company's contracted revenue base and provides the demand-side underpinning for the FY2026 revenue outlook. The acqui-hire of Lanteris's leadership and customer relationships is the mechanism by which the company competes for space-systems contracts against the Northrop Grummans and Raytheons of the world, not just against Firefly for the next CLPS task order.

| Adj. EBITDA | Negative | Positive |

## Structural concentration and the Artemis dependency

The customer concentration picture, stated plainly, is this: prior to the Lanteris acquisition, Intuitive Machines was a company whose revenue derived almost entirely from a single government programme administered by a single agency. CLPS is a well-structured programme with a large ceiling and genuine competitive discipline, but it is also a programme whose cadence, budget, and political durability are determined in Washington. The Artemis programme — the broader NASA initiative to return humans to the lunar surface — is the secular driver behind every CLPS task order, and Artemis's budget has faced recurring appropriations uncertainty.

The Lanteris acquisition addresses this concentration, but does not dissolve it. The combined company's satellite-systems business introduces commercial customers and defence-side government relationships that are not correlated with the Artemis budget cycle. Yet the $900 million to $1 billion FY2026 revenue outlook depends heavily on Lanteris's contribution — the three-to-four times implied year-on-year growth is an acquisition story as much as an organic one. The NASA Artemis programme remains the dominant secular driver of what Intuitive Machines ultimately becomes: if the agency sustains investment in lunar infrastructure through the decade, the CLPS ceiling is more than large enough to support a durable business. If appropriations compress, the counterparty addition Lanteris provides may prove to have been not merely a strategic enhancement but a structural necessity.
